units: a sky watched from a lit street looks almost bare
on a lonely plateau the same dome shows a swarm of stars
the whitish band then runs across the sky from one side to the other
the watcher also picks out different tints from one star to another
the gap between the two skies comes from the background, not the gear
the glow of the lamps wipes out the faintest objects
high up, dry air darkens the background of the sky
enthusiasts travel long distances to find darkness
text: Look up from a lit street and you would swear the sky is nearly bare. A dozen pale dots, a smear you can barely make out, and that is the whole show. Now carry those same eyes onto an empty plateau, far from any lamp post, and the dome fills with a swarm. The dots keep multiplying, the milky band runs clean across from one edge to the other, and your eye starts catching color, one star coppery here, another one bluish there. The gap between the two skies has nothing to do with your gear. It comes from the background. Down below, the glow of the lamps drowns the frailest stars and leaves a gray, hazy backdrop. Up high, dry air pushes that backdrop close to black, and the smallest spark stands out. That is why hobbyists drive for hours before they set up a tripod. They are not after a better telescope. They are after better dark.

units: the writer refuses to see near orbit treated as a dump
he lays out three sides of the problem
leftover launcher parts endanger working craft
highly reflective satellites spoil astronomical images
no operator carries the cost of cleaning up
the usual objection invokes the sheer size of the void
the writer answers that the lanes in use are narrow and overloaded
he concludes that a shared rulebook is missing
text: Low orbit should stop being treated as a dump with nobody watching it. Anyone willing to face the question squarely runs into three files. The first is debris: every rocket stage left behind turns into a projectile that threatens craft still doing their job. The second bears on watching from the ground, since bright strings of relay satellites streak across telescope plates and wreck whole measuring campaigns. The third gets discussed least. It is liability, because no operator picks up the cleanup bill it hands to whoever comes after. Someone will answer that space is vast, almost dizzying, and that the risk looks thin. The argument collapses the moment you look at the lanes actually in use, which are narrow and overloaded. A cluttered orbit is no engineering matter. It is a matter of shared rules, and those are missing.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: as a small child she watched the sky from the roof of her parents' farm
she wrote her observations down in a notebook
as a teenager she built an instrument herself from cardboard and salvaged lenses
the image came out shaky and dim, which suited her
she was later hired as an assistant at a high altitude observatory
she recorded where the comets stood through whole nights
once she ran the survey work she spotted an unknown moving body
she refused to let that object carry her family name
late in her career she urged newcomers to draw the real rather than the expected
text: As a small girl she climbed onto the flat roof of the family farm to follow one far-off star, a notebook balanced on her knees. In her teens she put a telescope together from a cardboard tube and two lenses salvaged out of a glazier's workshop. The image shook, it never came out sharp, and that was enough for her. A mountain observatory later took her on as an assistant, and she spent whole nights on end under a freezing sky, noting down where the comets stood. Once she ran the survey work she picked out a body nobody had reported, a thin point that shifted from one night to the next. She would never let it carry her family name. At the end of her working life she was still teaching beginners the one rule she thought sufficed: draw what you see, not what you hope to see.

units: the reviewer finds the mechanical design of the instrument faulty
the main mirror is held at three points only
that mounting warps the mirror and stretches the test star
the thin metal wall carries heat toward the inside of the optics
that heat stirs air currents which spoil the image at high power
the electronics box lets the damp of the night in
the damp eats away at the electrical contacts
the flaws pile up and drop the instrument to the rank of a beginner model
the remedies put forward cost little
text: The build of this telescope aimed at hobbyists deserves a hard look, since its mechanical choices set off one effect after another. The primary mirror rests on three pads and nothing more. Under its own weight it sags a little, so the test star spreads into an oval smudge instead of a clean disk. The tube, rolled from thin sheet metal, carries heat from the mount toward the optical axis, which feeds air currents inside and blurs the view at high power. The electronics box shuts badly and lets the night damp in, and the damp eats away at the contacts. Taken one at a time, each flaw would be bearable. Together they drag a scope sold as a performer down to the rank of a starter instrument. Putting it right costs almost nothing: a nine-point cell, insulation on the tube, a gasket on the box.

units: the request is made on behalf of an astronomy club
new lighting has gone up along the road bordering their site
observing sessions have become hard
part of the light output goes upward and creates a glare
faint objects turn invisible
members are losing heart and the workshops for newcomers are being dropped
the writers are not asking for the lighting to be taken away
they suggest hoods that aim the light at the ground and lower power at night
they invite the reader to come and see the nuisance after dark
text: I am writing on behalf of the observing society that meets on the plateau. Since fresh lighting went up along the road bordering our field, our sessions have turned into a trial. Part of the output from those lamps goes straight upward, and the glare it makes keeps us from picking out anything faint. Members are losing heart, and the workshops we run for newcomers are being dropped one after another. We are not asking for the stretch to go dark, nor for the work to be undone. A remedy already in use elsewhere would serve: fit each lamp with a hood that throws the light down onto the ground, then cut the power in the deep of the night. The outlay stays small, consumption falls, and the road loses none of its safety. We would gladly host a visit after dark, so that you can judge the nuisance yourself.

units: a rocky planet offers hard ground where a craft can land
a gas planet offers only a steady sinking toward denser layers
gas giants are far bulkier than solid planets
their heavy mass lets them keep a thick gas envelope
a rocky body would not hold that envelope
both categories form in the same starting disk
far from the star the cold binds ice and builds massive cores
those cores then draw in the surrounding gas
bare ground throws back a sharp glint while an atmosphere spreads a soft banded light
text: What sets a rocky planet apart from a gas planet? The first has a hard surface, rough underfoot, where a craft can actually set down. The second offers nothing but an endless fall through layers that keep thickening as you go. Are the two of them alike in size? Not in the least. The gas giants dwarf the solid globes, and their crushing mass holds on to a thick atmosphere that the pull of a rocky ball would simply let slip away. And where do the two come from? Both families grow out of one and the same disk, but far from the star the cold welds ice together, which builds cores heavy enough to trap the gas around them. Do we watch them the same way? Not quite. Barren ground throws back a hard glint, while a gas envelope spreads out a soft milky light in which you can make out bands.

units: the guide says right away that this session will differ from a usual screening

he then takes up the question of distances

the guide answers that its light takes more than four years to arrive
he traces how the instruments changed, from early wooden tubes to recent mirrors
he warns against looking at the face of the sun without protection
he ends with the craft sent far off with no way back
he notes that the oldest of them still travels beyond the planets on record
the audience listens without stirring
text: The guide warned us at the door that this would be no ordinary screening. He started with stars. Drop the idea of a fixed point, he said, and picture a ball of gas burning itself up. Then he took up distances. A woman beside us asked whether the nearest star could be seen at all. Yes, he said, though its light takes more than four years to reach us. After that he walked us through the instruments, from the wooden tubes of the early days to the mirrors of today. He paused on the dark patches on the face of the sun and told us never to aim at it without a filter, or we would burn our eyes. He ended with the probes, craft sent off toward something distant with no way home. The oldest of them, he added, is still rolling through the void, well past the planets on record. Nobody in the room stirred.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before the first spyglasses the sky was mapped without any optical instrument
the positions of the bright stars were entered in tables

the arrival of optical instruments revealed objects unknown until then
the lists of objects grew much longer
the trade moved from describing to measuring
photography made it possible to record stars invisible to the eye
charts stopped being drawn by hand
electronic detectors turn out inventories too vast for a single team
text: Long before anyone ground a lens, watchers were already mapping the sky with the naked eye, entering the places of the brightest stars in tables. Those records steered ships and carved up the year. Then came the age of glass instruments, and the dome filled with objects nobody had suspected: spots, rings, moons. The lists swelled, and the trade changed character, because measuring now counted as much as describing. The photographic plate tipped the discipline over. A long exposure brought out stars too frail for the eye, and charts stopped being drawn by hand. Later still, electronic detectors and automated surveys turned out inventories so huge that no single team could ever work through them. The dome overhead has not changed. What has changed is the way we set it down.

units: the twinkling does not come from the stars themselves
it happens in the air above the watcher
layers of air at different temperatures mix there without pause
each layer bends the beam that crosses it
the shifting path gives an impression of wobbling and changing tint
a planet shows a small disk instead of a single point
the rays from that disk cancel one another and the light looks steady
watchers draw from this a way to tell a near body from a far one
calm air brings out the finest detail
astronomers wait for those steady moments to record their images
text: That shiver we hand to the stars is not theirs at all. It is born in the air we breathe, high above our heads. Warm and cold masses of air mix up there without pause, and each one bends the beam that crosses it, the way an uneven pane of glass would. The ray reaches us along a path that keeps moving, so the star seems to shudder, to flare and fade, to turn coppery and then blue. A planet shows a tiny disk instead of a single point. Its many rays cancel one another out, and its light holds steady. Hence the rule watchers keep: what twinkles is far off, what burns without a tremor is close. When the air settles, the dome sharpens, and the finest detail that all the churning had rubbed out comes through at last. Watchers wait for those lulls and trip the shutter right then.

units: the drive mechanism fails during a run of exposures
with no drive the instrument no longer offsets the spin of our world
the images come out as streaks instead of points
the man in charge suspects a power supply fault at first
measuring the voltage rules that out
the real cause is a gear with worn teeth that slips
the repair would have taken a week, which the passing of the comet ruled out
the team shortens every exposure and then stacks the frames by computer
the outcome, less precise, still allows the motion of the body to be measured
text: The night promised to be a fine one when the drive motor quit, halfway through a run of exposures. With nothing driving it, the tube stopped offsetting the spin of our world, and every frame came out streaked instead of dotted. The man in charge of the dome suspected the power supply first, then measured the voltage, which read fine. The fault lay in a gear whose teeth had worn down until they slipped under load. Swapping the part meant a week of waiting, and the comet was not going to hold still that long. So the team cut each exposure to whatever the mount could carry without visible drift, then stacked the frames by computer. The outcome came out coarser than hoped, yet it served to measure how the nucleus moved. The lesson fit in one line: a mechanical failure can also be got around in processing.
